newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong defends plans for 1998 elections.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong defends plans for 1998 elections.

text.p: Hong Kong's post-colonial government on Tuesday defended its plans for "open and fair" elections next year and said it hoped to have new electoral rules in place by the end of August.
The new government challenged critics to substantiate their claims that the legislative elections, the territory's first under Chinese rule, would not be open.

Michael Suen, speaking in his new capacity as secretary for constitutional affairs, said the government hoped to push through new electoral rules soon in preparation for polls in the second quarter of 1998.

Suen, Hong Kong's former secretary for home affairs, said the government would table draft rules in two weeks before the China-appointed Provisional Legislative Council (PLC) and hoped they would become law by end August.
The PLC replaced an elected assembly on July 1, when Britain handed over this former colony of 156 years back to China.
"It's all very well for them to say that they fear it won't be open and fair, but they have got to substantiate it," Suen said on government-funded radio.
Elections in Hong Kong, particularly the last two, had been widely accepted as fair and open and Suen said he could not understand the present scepticism.
"I don't see why people continue to suspect our intentions and cast doubts on the frankness and openness of our system."
Suen's comments follow Britain's remarks last week that it hoped Hong Kong would hold free and fair elections soon.
London had also pledged to ensure freedoms are maintained and that the high degree of autonomy as promised to Hong Kong under Sino-British treaties on its handover is honoured.

Under the new electoral plan, Hong Kong will dump the first-past-the-post method, opting instead that 20 of the 60-seat chamber be directly elected from geographical constituencies through proportional representation.
The territory will be divided into five constituencies, each with three to five seats depending on the population.
In the last legislative polls in 1995, the territory was divided into 20 smaller geographical constituencies, each of which was allocated one seat.
But critics of the new system have predicted that pro-democracy parties are unlikely to repeat their strong 1995 showing in which they won the largest bloc of seats in the ousted colonial assembly.
In the new plan, functional constituencies will return 30 seats while another 10 will be elected from a committee formed with 800 permanent Hong Kong residents from different sectors.
